examples.question_text: Which of $\sqrt{11}$, $\sqrt{64}$ and $\sqrt{19}$ are surds? Explain.
examples.solution_text:
$\sqrt{64}=8$, so it is rational and not a surd.
$11$ and $19$ are not perfect squares, so their square roots are irrational.
The surds are $\sqrt{11}$ and $\sqrt{19}$.

examples.question_text:
Decide whether each root is a surd. Explain.
a. $\sqrt[3]{12}$
b. $\sqrt[3]{216}$
c. $\sqrt[4]{625}$
examples.solution_text:
a. $2^{3}=8$ and $3^{3}=27$. Since $8<12<27$, $12$ is not a perfect cube. Its cube root is irrational, so $\sqrt[3]{12}$ is a surd.
b. $6^{3}=216$, so $\sqrt[3]{216}=6$. It is rational and not a surd.
c. $5^{4}=625$, so $\sqrt[4]{625}=5$. It is rational and not a surd.

examples.question_text: Decide whether $\sqrt[3]{-64}$ and $\sqrt[3]{-20}$ are surds. Explain.
examples.solution_text:
Both roots are real because their index is odd.
$(-4)^{3}=-64$, so $\sqrt[3]{-64}=-4$. It is rational and not a surd.
$(-3)^{3}=-27$ and $(-2)^{3}=-8$. Since $-27<-20<-8$, $-20$ is not a perfect cube. Its cube root is irrational, so $\sqrt[3]{-20}$ is a surd.

examples.question_text:
Classify each expression as a surd or rational. Explain.
a. $3\sqrt{7}$
b. $2-\sqrt{11}$
c. $4+\sqrt{36}$
d. $\frac{5\sqrt{16}}{3}$
examples.solution_text:
a. $7$ is not a perfect square, so $\sqrt{7}$ is irrational. Multiplying it by the nonzero rational number $3$ leaves it irrational. $3\sqrt{7}$ is a surd.
b. $\sqrt{11}$ is irrational. Subtracting it from the rational number $2$ leaves an irrational value. $2-\sqrt{11}$ is a surd.
c. $\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}4+\sqrt{36}\\&=4+6\\&=10\end{aligned}$
The expression is rational.
d. $\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{5\sqrt{16}}{3}\\&=\frac{5\times4}{3}\\&=\frac{20}{3}\end{aligned}$
The expression is rational because it is a fraction of two integers.

examples.question_text:
Classify each root as a surd, rational, or not real. Explain.
a. $\sqrt{\frac{25}{144}}$
b. $\sqrt{\frac{17}{64}}$
c. $\sqrt{-25}$
d. $\sqrt{0}$
examples.solution_text:
a. $\frac{25}{144}=\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^{2}$, so $\sqrt{\frac{25}{144}}=\frac{5}{12}$. The root is rational.
b. $\frac{17}{64}$ is in simplest form. Its denominator is a perfect square but its numerator is not, so it is not the square of a rational number. $\sqrt{\frac{17}{64}}$ is a surd.
c. No real number squares to a negative number. $\sqrt{-25}$ is not real.
d. $\sqrt{0}=0$. Zero is rational, so this root is not a surd.

examples.question_text: Using a calculator, approximate $\sqrt{15}$ to $2$ decimal places. State its exact value.
examples.solution_text:
$\sqrt{15}=3.872983\ldots$
The third decimal digit is $2$, so round down.
$\sqrt{15}\approx3.87$ to $2$ decimal places.
Its exact value is $\sqrt{15}$. The rounded decimal $3.87$ is an approximation.

examples.question_text: Mia says that every square root is a surd and that a fractional number under the root must give an irrational answer. Use $\sqrt{100}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{36}{49}}$ to explain why both claims are incorrect.
examples.solution_text:
$\sqrt{100}=10$, which is rational. A root sign alone does not make a surd.
$\frac{36}{49}=\left(\frac{6}{7}\right)^{2}$, so $\sqrt{\frac{36}{49}}=\frac{6}{7}$, which is also rational.
A square root is a surd when its value is irrational. A fractional radicand can be the square of a rational number.

coverage.summary: Authored seven worked examples covering all distinct retained assessment methods, using different values and supplied teaching evidence. Questions and solutions are separate; prose remains editable and inherits automatic blue solution styling. Relation-led calculations have phantom equals gutters. No diagrams are needed for these classification and rounding tasks. Practice and quiz mathematics were unchanged and were read only for method mapping. Actual rendering and typography verification remain for the later visual stage.

examples.derivation: 8²=64; 9<11<16 and 16<19<25. Thus √64=8 is rational, while √11 and √19 are surds. The supplied source card activity supports selecting irrational roots from a list.
2³=8<12<27=3³, so ∛12 is irrational. 6³=216 and 5⁴=625, giving rational roots 6 and 5. Matching perfect-power classification follows the supplied definition for integer indices n≥2.
(-4)³=-64, so ∛(-64)=-4 is rational. (-3)³=-27<-20<-8=(-2)³; -20 is not an integer cube, so its cube root is irrational. Both roots are real because their index is odd.

√7 and √11 are irrational. Nonzero rational scaling gives irrational 3√7, and rational subtraction gives irrational 2-√11. Independently, 4+√36=4+6=10 and 5√16/3=5×4/3=20/3 are rational. Both continuation calculations have appropriate phantom equals gutters.

25/144=(5/12)², so its principal square root is 5/12. The reduced fraction 17/64 is not a rational square because 17 is not a square; its positive root is a surd. No real square is negative, so √(-25) is not real. √0=0 is rational.
√15=3.872983346… . The third decimal digit is 2, giving 3.87 to two decimal places. √15 remains the exact value; 3.87 is an approximation.

10²=100 and (6/7)²=36/49. Their principal square roots are the rational values 10 and 6/7. These counterexamples independently refute both claims using the source's classification and fractional-radicand methods.

No existing examples require retention review. Single-dollar mathematics, separate editable prose and solution fields, and authored gutters comply with the supplied conventions. No diagrams or syllabus exceptions are required. Rendering verification remains for the later visual stage; practice and quiz mathematics were not re-audited.
